cells.tense: Now the thing is done, and the release is happening here, in the room.
cells.act: tend it small and ask nothing of it
cells.ask: Go back once to what's finished — a little attention, no pushing it forward, no verdict on how it turned out. Let it stay the size it is. That's the whole ask.
cells.core:
In the body, endings happen on schedule for you. Something lands, and you can set it down the same day — no ceremony, no carrying it around to check whether it still fits. That is rare. Most people need a reason. Yours arrives with the finish line.

The easy next thing is the other half. When one closes, you can step toward the next with a light hand, meeting it as it is this week instead of what you already want it to become. Tend it small. Ask nothing from it yet.

If you catch yourself building the next one before it is needed, that's the cue to keep your attention on the version already here.

cells.tense: You are already putting down things that haven't finished happening yet.
cells.act: keep the session even when it feels pointless
cells.ask: Stay with an unfinished piece through the plain daily session — same piece, same small round, even on the day it shows you nothing. No result to reach for, no deadline.
cells.core:
Where something is being carried through, things get set down before they are done. You can hand over the result, step back, call it finished — and from the outside it looks like grace. Inside, it's a jump. Whatever isn't finished gets left in the middle and named acceptance.

So stay with the smallest real piece of it. Alone, no audience, no improvement plan — the plain version, one more round on the day it feels pointless. The ending is made there. It's slower than releasing early, and it holds what releasing early keeps dropping.

The pull to declare things done early will stay a while. Repeating the plain piece is what keeps the actual ending on time.

cells.tense: You were holding something that had already finished, and the arm is still up.
cells.act: hold your shape under the weight
cells.ask: With something you're still carrying, keep your shape under it for an hour — no fix, no verdict, nothing set down. Stay the same size; let the weight keep its size.
cells.core:
Something finished, and you're still carrying it. The grip shows in the body first — shoulders, jaw, the way you keep hold of something whose ending already happened. You've been at it so long the tension reads as who you are.

This week, stay with what you carry for an hour without deciding anything about it. Not release — just the hour, at its real size. Being strong at holding is not the problem. The problem is holding past the ending.

If the hour feels like nothing, that is the sign the strength is already there and only needs to be pointed at something that can receive it.

cells.tense: You have been releasing something without knowing the releasing was yours.
cells.act: give it what it needs today, not what it is scheduled for
cells.ask: To something you've stepped back from, give what today actually asks rather than what the old plan says. A small act, no announcement, no clock — done whenever you get to it.
cells.core:
You've loosened your grip here, and you're the last to know. You stepped back somewhere months ago — in a role, a rhythm, the way you used to run things — and you tell it as if you were pushed. The setdown happened. Nobody has put a name on it.

So take something you've quietly stepped away from and give it what today asks, not what the old plan says. A small attentive act, no announcement. That's what care looks like when it isn't steering.

Whether or not you chalk it up to circumstance, the hand still in it is steady. This is a chance to see that.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is holding something they know the shape of — I name chronic holding but never what is held or for how long, and the record permits none of that. A reader could reasonably say the holding is a season, not a habit, and that stopping would cost them something real; so every ask must be doable inside the grip, not contingent on dropping it. The ask survives my being wrong about the pattern because it only asks for one act, witnessed and unhurried, and is useful even to someone who is not stuck. The sentence serving the writer over the person is 'you have already let go and not noticed,' which flatters the reader's insight and presumes their inner state — it is gone from the cells.
